title: Katha Upanishad (one week): Nachiketa and Death (6 of 7)
hook: arise, awake; the path is sharp as a razor's edge
carry: choose the good over the pleasant
tomorrow: Katha Upanishad (one week): Nachiketa and Death (7 of 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday, ratha: the chariot of the self. Rider, charioteer, reins and horses.

Ever been woken by someone who really needed you up? Not a gentle alarm. A hand on the shoulder, a voice: get up, now. One verse in the Katha sounds exactly like that: short, urgent, impossible to sleep through. Swami Vivekananda took it up as a rallying cry for his listeners. It's possible to know the line well without knowing it came from the house of Death.
screen: `A HAND ON THE SHOULDER.` → `GET UP, NOW.` → `FROM THE HOUSE OF DEATH.`

segments.voice: Right after the chariot, Yama says: uttishthata, jagrata. Arise! Awake! Having reached the great teachers, learn. Then a warning: the path is sharp as the edge of a razor, hard to cross, hard to walk, say the wise. Step carelessly and you're cut. That doesn't make it cruel. It makes it narrow. Choosing the good over the pleasant isn't done once; it's done step by step, with attention. A few verses later, Yama explains why the path is hard. The self-existent one, he says, pierced the openings of the senses outward. So eyes, ears and attention point away, by design, not at the self within. But some wise person, wishing for the deathless, turned their eyes inward and saw the self. The phrase is often translated as turning the gaze around. And what's seen? A person the size of a thumb, dwelling in the middle of the body, like a flame without smoke. Lord of past and future. The same today and tomorrow. Three ways of saying one thing. Arise, awake: the sleeper drifts toward the pleasant. The razor's edge: the good path is narrow and needs care. The inward gaze: the senses face out, and the good path turns them back. None of it is gloomy. A flame without smoke is a warm picture, and it's what's waiting when you stop looking only outward.
screen: `ARISE! AWAKE!` · `SHARP AS A RAZOR'S EDGE.` · `THE SENSES FACE OUTWARD.` · `A FLAME WITHOUT SMOKE.` · then, large: `TURN THE GAZE AROUND.`

segments.voice: Open your eyes and notice how naturally they go outward, to the room, the light, whatever moves. Now close them and turn the gaze around: not looking at anything, just feeling the place you look from. If it helps, picture a small, steady flame in the center of the chest, smokeless and warm; if not, simply rest behind your closed eyes.
Uttishthata, arise. The good path is sharp as a razor's edge, and it turns the gaze inward. Awake, and learn.
Your line: choose the good over the pleasant. The good path is narrow, not cruel. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Katha 1.3.14, 'uttishthata jagrata', was taken up by Swami Vivekananda as a call to awaken, and Hindu teachers quote it as a call to wake up to the self.

match.prompt: three ways of saying it — tap the pairs.
pairs: the path is narrow, hard to walk

myth: 'arise, awake' was first said by Vivekananda
it's Katha 1.3.14; Vivekananda made it famous in modern India.
the Katha says the senses were made to face outward
so we look outward, not within; the wise turn the gaze around.

fork.setup: your senses all face outward. you want to see the self. what does the wise person in the Katha do?
fork.reveal: wishing for the deathless, the wise one turned the eyes inward, and saw the self.

original.note: Sanskrit: uttishthata, arise! (plural); Katha 1.3.14: uttishthata jagrata, arise, awake.

trapdoor: what you thought: 'arise, awake' is a modern motivational slogan.
what it means: it's Death's call to wake up to the self, on a path sharp as a razor's edge.
what a scholar hears: 1.3.14 continues prapya varan nibodhata, having reached the great ones, learn; 2.1.1 says the self-existent pierced the senses outward (parañci khani).
guess: a call to stand up, to rise
a call to sit down and be still
a call to give thanks and rest
